Spring vs tween, same target

A damped spring, solved in closed form, against a fixed 700 ms bezier tween, pulling the same dot across the same rail. Same target, same weight; different answer to “what happens after it arrives”.

What to watch

  • Overshoot is quantified, not tuned. ζ = 0.64 predicts an overshoot of exp(−ζπ/√(1−ζ²)) = 7.35%; the closed form reports 7.354% at 373 ms — the two agree to three decimals, which is what an exact solution of a linear oscillator should do. The bezier tween cannot overshoot at all — its control points are pinned inside the box — so "springy" and "tweened" are distinguishable by measurement, not by taste.
  • The tails differ in kind. Every half cycle the spring keeps 7.35% of the previous deviation: +7.3%, then −0.54%, then +0.04%. It is inside ±0.5% at 785 ms and inside ±0.1% at 943 ms — and to be inside ±0.01% takes 1299 ms. Any stricter definition just buys another half cycle. The tween is done at 700 ms, exactly, forever. A spring has no end; a tween has nothing but an end.
  • Flip the target mid-flight. Press the button while both dots are moving. The spring keeps its velocity through the retarget and turns around on a curve; the tween has no velocity to keep — it restarts its timing function from wherever it is, so its speed drops to zero in one frame. The restart counter under the right track counts that discontinuity. This is the difference that shows up in real UI and is invisible in a single-run demo.
  • Peak speeds are closer than the feel suggests. Spring peaks at 5.28 track/s at 104 ms, the tween at 6.49 — yet the tween reads as the faster of the two, because speed at the end and at the start is what the eye integrates, and the tween spends 700 ms accelerating then falling to a dead stop.
Where this is not your engine. The spring here is the exact solution of a linear damped oscillator, with no clamping, no rest threshold and no velocity cap. Production spring libraries (iOS UISpringTimingParameters, Framer Motion, react-spring) integrate numerically and add a rest threshold and a maximum duration; those change the settle time you measure, not the shape. tools/measure.py runs the same parameters through a 2 kHz semi-implicit Euler and reports where it lands — up to 0.21% of the rail off, and 5 ms early on the ±0.5% crossing. The tween assumes a re-target resets the timing function and drops velocity — true of CSS transitions and of most JS tweeners, false of engines that blend velocities across retargets.
